title: Exercise and Your Heart
summary: How the heart pumps blood around the body, why it beats faster during exercise, and how being active every day makes it stronger.
poll: Playing outside is just as important for children as doing homework.

versions.title: Your Busy Heart
versions.text:
Put your hand on your chest. Do you feel a thump? That is your heart.

Your heart is a muscle. It is as big as your fist. It pumps blood all day and all night. It never stops.

Blood goes all through your body. It moves in thin tubes. It takes air and food to each part of you.

When you rest, your heart beats about 70 to 100 times a minute. You can feel each beat. Press two fingers on your wrist. That beat is your pulse.

Now run fast. Your legs need more air. So your heart beats fast. You breathe hard, too.

Exercise makes your heart strong, just like your arms and legs. A strong heart pumps more blood in each beat. So it does not have to work as hard.

Kids need to move a lot. Try to play hard for one hour each day. You can run, swim, ride a bike, or play ball. Do not sit for too long.

In Saudi Arabia, the days can be hot. Play in the cool part of the day. Drink lots of water. Your heart will thank you!

versions.title: Exercise and Your Heart
versions.text:
Place your hand on the left side of your chest and stay still for a moment. Can you feel a steady thump? That is your heart, and it has been working since before you were born.

Your heart is a muscle about the size of your fist. It pumps blood day and night, even while you sleep, and it never takes a break.

Blood travels around your body through tubes called blood vessels. It carries oxygen from the air you breathe, along with nutrients from food, to every part of you.

When you are resting, a child's heart usually beats about 70 to 100 times a minute. You can feel these beats by pressing two fingers gently on your wrist or the side of your neck. This beat is called your pulse. To measure it, count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply by four.

Now imagine you are running in a race. Your leg muscles suddenly need extra oxygen, so your heart beats faster to deliver more blood. You also breathe harder to pull in more air.

Exercise that makes you breathe hard for a long time is called aerobic exercise. It makes your heart stronger, the same way lifting makes your arms stronger. A strong heart pumps more blood with each beat, so it does not need to beat as often when you rest.

Doctors say children should be active for at least 60 minutes every day. Running, swimming, cycling, jumping rope, and playing football are all excellent choices. It also helps to spend less time sitting in front of screens.

In Saudi Arabia, summer days can be extremely hot, so it is wise to exercise during the cooler morning or evening, or indoors. Always drink plenty of water. Your heart will thank you!

versions.title: Exercise and Your Heart
versions.text:
Place your hand on the left side of your chest and remain completely still for a moment. Can you feel a steady, rhythmic thump? That is your heart, which has been working continuously since before you were born.

Your heart is a muscular organ approximately the size of your fist, and together with your blood vessels it forms your cardiovascular system. It pumps blood day and night, even while you are asleep, and it never rests.

Blood must circulate through an enormous network of vessels, delivering oxygen from the air you breathe, together with nutrients from your food, to every cell in your body.

When you are resting, a child's heart typically beats about 70 to 100 times per minute. You can detect these beats, which together form your pulse, by pressing two fingers gently against your wrist or the side of your neck. To measure your heart rate, count the beats for 15 seconds and then multiply the total by four.

During vigorous activity, such as sprinting in a race, your leg muscles demand additional oxygen, so your heart accelerates to deliver more blood. Simultaneously, you breathe more deeply to draw in extra air.

Regular aerobic exercise, which keeps you breathing hard for an extended period, strengthens your heart in the same way that lifting weights strengthens your arms. It also builds endurance, the ability to keep going without tiring quickly. A stronger heart pumps more blood with every contraction, so it does not need to beat as frequently at rest.

Medical experts recommend that children be physically active for at least 60 minutes daily. Running, swimming, cycling, jumping rope, and football are all excellent choices. In contrast, a sedentary lifestyle, with long hours of sitting in front of screens, can weaken the heart over time.

In Saudi Arabia, summer temperatures can be extremely high, so it is sensible to exercise during the cooler morning or evening hours, or indoors, and to drink plenty of water. Your heart will be grateful!

versions.title: Exercise and Your Heart
versions.text:
Place your hand on the left side of your chest and remain completely still for a moment, and you will probably detect a steady, rhythmic thump. That sensation is produced by your heart, an extraordinary organ that has been functioning continuously since before you were born.

Your heart is a muscular organ approximately the size of your fist, and together with your blood vessels it constitutes your cardiovascular system, which transports blood day and night, even while you are asleep, without ever pausing to rest.

Blood must circulate through an extensive network of vessels, delivering oxygen from the air you inhale, together with nutrients absorbed from your digested food, to every individual cell in your body, from the delicate tissues of your brain to the tips of your toes.

When you are resting, a child's heart typically beats approximately 70 to 100 times per minute. You can detect these beats, which collectively constitute your pulse, by pressing two fingers gently against your wrist or the side of your neck. You can calculate your heart rate by counting the beats for 15 seconds and multiplying the total by four.

During vigorous physical activity, such as sprinting in a competitive race, your leg muscles demand considerably more oxygen, so your heart accelerates to deliver additional blood, while your breathing simultaneously deepens and quickens so that your lungs can absorb extra oxygen from the atmosphere.

Regular aerobic exercise, which keeps you breathing hard for an extended period, strengthens your heart in the same way that lifting weights strengthens your arms. It also develops endurance, the capacity to continue an activity without becoming exhausted quickly. Because a well-conditioned heart pumps more blood with every contraction, it does not need to beat as frequently at rest, which allows it to operate more efficiently throughout your life.

Medical experts consequently recommend that children participate in moderate or energetic physical activity for at least 60 minutes daily. Running, swimming, cycling, jumping rope, and football are all excellent possibilities. In contrast, a sedentary lifestyle, characterized by prolonged periods of sitting in front of televisions, computers, and other electronic screens, can gradually weaken the cardiovascular system, because muscles that are rarely challenged tend to lose their strength.

In Saudi Arabia, summer temperatures can become extremely high, so it is sensible to exercise during the cooler morning or evening hours, or in air-conditioned facilities, and to drink plenty of water before, during, and after physical activity. Your heart will be grateful!

wrong.C: The article says both have effects.
wrong.D: Endurance comes from activity, not sitting.

questions.stem: A student wants to build endurance before a long school race. Which plan best matches the article?
options: Run regularly for long periods
Sprint once a month as fast as possible, then rest
Watch videos of famous athletes for an hour a day
Avoid drinking water so the body gets used to thirst
questions.why: Endurance develops through regular aerobic exercise that keeps you breathing hard for a long time.

wrong.B: Once a month is not regular exercise.
wrong.D: The article advises drinking plenty of water.

questions.stem: Why does the author include advice about exercising in Saudi Arabia's summer?
options: To argue that people should not live in hot places
To show that the heart works differently in Saudi Arabia
To give a local, practical way to follow the advice safely
To list the hottest cities in the country
questions.why: The final paragraph adapts the general advice to the local climate so readers can exercise safely.

wrong.A: The article makes no such argument.
wrong.D: No cities are listed.
